title: Cc No. 7842/2017 Icici Bank vs Sachin Singh Thakur Page 1 Of 29 on 23 October, 2020
full_text: Cc No. 7842/2017 Icici Bank vs Sachin Singh Thakur Page 1 Of 29 on 23 October, 2020 IN THE COURT OF Ms. SHRUTI CHAUDHARY, METROPOLITAN MAGISTRATE (N.I. ACT)-02, PATIALA HOUSE COURTS: NEW DELHI DLND020203792016 Case No: 7842/2017 ICICI Bank Limited ICICI Bank Limited Having its registered office at: Landmark, Race Course Circle, Vadodara-390007 and having its branch office at: Videocon Tower, 2nd Floor, E-Block, Jhandewalan Extension, Through Its Authorized Representative ....... Complainant Versus Sachin Kumar Thakur A 5/101, Block A, PKT-5, Sector-17, Rohini, Delhi-110085 Also At: Sachin Singh Thakur Flat No. 101, First Floor, Nikhil Woodland Apartments Mauza Kakretha Mauza Kaketha, Agra, Uttar Pradesh-282001 Also At: Sachin Singh Thakur B-68, GK Part-1 New Delhi-110048 ....... Accused CC No. 7842/2017 ICICI Bank vs Sachin Singh Thakur Page 1 of 29 Date of Filing: 06.10.2016 Offence Complained of: 138 NI Act Plea of the Accused: Not Guilty Decision: Acquitted Date of Judgment: 23.10.2020 JUDGMENT 1. Vide this judgment, I shall decide the complaint case bearing CC no. 7842/2017. Brief facts of the present complaint filed u/s 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (hereinafter, NI Act ) is that the complainant is a banking company offering banking, financing and loan facilities to its customers for purchase of vehicles, machinery etc. It is averred by the complainant that the accused had availed finance facilities from the complainant bank under home loan schemes vide loan agreement number LBDEL00002184163, however, defaulted in making regular payment of monthly installments. 2. It is further stated that in partial discharge of his admitted debts and liabilities, the complainant had issued a cheque bearing no. 000022 dated 22.08.2016 for an amount of Rs. 14,25,000/- in favour of the complainant, which was returned unpaid upon deposition with remarks "funds insufficient" vide return memo dated 23.08.2016. 3. Legal demand notice dated 12.09.2016 was sent to the accused by the complainant; however, no payment was made by the accused within 15 days of the receipt of the notice. Hence, the present complaint. CC No. 7842/2017 ICICI Bank vs Sachin Singh Thakur Page 2 of 29 4. AR of the complainant, Sh. Lokesh Jaiman, entered into evidence certain documents in his pre-summoning evidence by way of affidavit, which are as follows: Sr. No. Documents Exhibited As: 1. Power of Attorney Ex. CW-1/A 2. Cheque in question Ex. CW-1/B 3. Cheque return memo Ex. CW-1/C 4. Copy of legal demand notice Ex. CW-1/D 5. Postal receipt and delivery report Ex. CW-1/E 6. Complaint Ex.CW-1/F 7. Evidence by way of affidavit Ex. CW-1/1 5. As all the ingredients of Section 138 NI Act were fulfilled by the complainant, summons was issued against the accused on 30.05.2017, who entered upon his appearance on 29.08.2018. Notice of accusation was served upon the accused on the same day and the plea of defence taken by the accused was that there was no legal debt or liability against the complainant. The accused further stated in his plea of defence that at the time of signing of tripartite agreement, the official of complainant bank had taken nine blank signed cheques as security from the accused with the assurance that the same would not be presented without the written consent of the accused, however, the cheque in question is one of the above nine cheques which has been illegally and unlawfully presented without the express consent of the accused. 6. An application u/s 145 (2) NI Act was filed on behalf of the accused which was allowed by this court. Cross examination of CW-1, AR of the complainant, took place on 19.03.2019 and 08.08.2019 respectively. In the cross examination, inter alia, CW-1 stated that the home loan facility was disbursed to the accused on a floating rate of interest. CW-1 answered to a question posed on behalf of the CC No. 7842/2017 ICICI Bank vs Sachin Singh Thakur Page 3 of 29 accused regarding clear title pertaining to the house in question, stating that the loan was disbursed on allotment basis and that the bank was not liable to check for clear title. 7. CW-1 further expressed his inability to recognize the cheque in question as being one of the nine blank signed cheuqes given to the complainant bank at the time of entering into the tripartite agreement. CW-1 further could not state clearly whether the nine blank signed cheques were given for miscellaneous and pre- EMI charges, however, clearly stated that 'as per credit policy, one has to deposit four cheques at the time of disbursal of loan. One of the cheques is a cancelled cheque and the other three cheques are to be given as security cheques.' 8. CE stood closed on 08.08.2019. All the incriminating evidence led in CE was put to the accused and the statement of accused u/s 313 r/w 281 Cr.PC was recorded on 08.08.2019, wherein the accused reiterated his defence that no legal debt or liability exists on his part in favour of the complainant. Accused agreed to lead evidence. 9. Thereafter, DE was conducted on 03.10.2019, 02.12.2019 and was finally closed on 29.01.2020. Ld. Counsel for the complainant duly cross examined the accused. DW-1 stated that the loan was given by the complainant bank to the accused after a margin money was already paid by the accused to the builder and then later DW-1 changed his testimony stating that the loan was given before the payment of margin money to the builder. DW-1 further stated in his cross- examination that the nine cheques were forcefully taken from him towards the payment of loan charges, title report charges, pre-EMI charges etc. DW-1 further denied that any amount of Rs. 5000/- was not paid by him to the complainant bank towards title search report charges. He further stated that no legal demand notice was received by him, although, it was sent to the correct residential CC No. 7842/2017 ICICI Bank vs Sachin Singh Thakur Page 4 of 29 address of the accused, which was provided by the accused to the bank at the time of availing of the said home loan facility. DE stood closed on 29.01.2020. 10. Final arguments were led and written arguments were filed on behalf of both parties on the official e-mail Id of this court i.e. readermmni02@phc. I have heard both parties at length, considered the evidence led by them and thoroughly perused the documents on record. 11. The present complaint has been filed u/s 138 NI Act. The complainant has alleged that an offence u/s 138 NI Act has been committed by the accused, which is being reproduced here for perusal: "138 Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc., of funds in the account. --Where any cheque drawn by a person on an account maintained by him with a banker for payment of any amount of money to another person from out of that account for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability, is returned by the bank unpaid, either because of the amount of money standing to the credit of that account is insufficient to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account by an agreement made with that bank, such person shall be deemed to have committed an offence and shall, without prejudice to any other provisions of this Act, be punished with imprisonment for a term which may be extended to two years, or with fine which may extend to twice the amount of the cheque, or with both: Provided that nothing contained in this section shall apply unless-- (a) the cheque has been presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity, whichever is earlier; (b) the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque, as the case may be, makes a demand for the payment of the said amount of money by giving a notice in writing, to the drawer of the cheque, within thirty days of the receipt of information by him from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid; and (c) the drawer of such cheque fails to make the payment of the said amount of money to the payee or, as the case may be, to the holder in due course of the cheque, within fifteen days of the receipt of the CC No. 7842/2017 ICICI Bank vs Sachin Singh Thakur Page 5 of 29 said notice. Explanation. -- For the purposes of this section, "debt or other liability" means a legally enforceable debt or other liability." 12. The accused has not disputed his signatures on the cheque in question. It is a well- settled law that once signature on the cheque is not disputed by the accused, the rebuttable presumption u/s 118 (a) and s.139 NI Act, of existence of legally enforceable debt on part of the accused, arises which are being quoted below for ready referral: "118 Presumptions as to negotiable instruments. --Until the contrary is proved, the following presumptions shall be made: -- (a) of consideration --that every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration, and that every such instrument, when it has been accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred, was accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred for consideration; (b) as to date --that every negotiable instrument bearing a date was made or drawn on such date; (c) as to time of acceptance --that every accepted bill of exchange was accepted within a reasonable time after its date and before its maturity; (d) as to time of transfer --that every transfer of a negotiable instrument was made before its maturity; (e) as to order of indorsements --that the indorsements appearing upon a negotiable instrument were made in the order in which they appear thereon; (f) as to stamps --that a lost promissory note, bill of exchange or cheque was duly stamped; (g) that holder is a holder in due course --that the holder of a negotiable instrument is a holder in due course: Provided that, where the instrument has been obtained from its lawful owner, or from any person in lawful custody thereof, by means of an offence or fraud, or has been obtained from the maker or acceptor thereof by means of an offence or fraud, or for unlawful consideration, the burden of proving that the holder is a holder in due course lies upon him." 139. Presumption in favour of holder. --It shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that the holder of a cheque received the cheque of the nature referred to in section 138 for the CC No. 7842/2017 ICICI Bank vs Sachin Singh Thakur Page 6 of 29 discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability. 13. Relying upon the case of Rangappa vs Srimohan (2010) 11 SCC 441, the statutory presumption is raised in favour of the complainant that the cheque in question was issued by the accused to the complainant for the discharge of any debt or other liability. Now, keeping in mind the observations of the Apex Court in Kali Ram vs. State of Himachal Pradesh , (1973) 2 SCC 808 the onus is now upon the accused to rebut the above presumption by bringing on record such "probable defence" which is consistent with his innocence. It is further clear that the accused need not even step into the witness box to raise these probable defences and can rebut the same by placing reliance on the material brought on record by the complainant. 14. Therefore, in the present matter, the onus of proof has now shifted upon the accused to raise a probable defence and to rebut the presumption of the existence of a legally recoverable debt arisen in favour of the complainant company. Now, let us examine the defences raised by the accused and evaluate the same. CASE OF THE ACCUSED 15. It is the case of the accused that he wished to purchase a flat no.101, 3BHK, (SBUA-1575 Sq. Ft.) (henceforth, "the flat") developed by Kunal Structural Developers & Industries Pvt. Ltd. under their project named "Nikhil Woodland Apartment" situated at Kakretha, Agra, valued at Rs. 53,00,000/- (Rupees Fifty- three lac only). It was for this purpose that the accused had approached the complainant bank after making a payment of Rs. 6,40,000/- (out of Rs. 8,00,000) towards deposit/ margin money/ own contribution to the builder. The accused avers that the complainant bank sanctioned a loan of Rs. 42,75,000/- and disbursed the amount of Rs. 42,35,000/- to the builder, which was 99% of the sanctioned amount, in a lump sum manner. CC No. 7842/2017 ICICI Bank vs Sachin Singh Thakur Page 7 of 29 16. The accused states that the present complaint is not maintainable as the same is based on a fraudulent property transaction wherein the complainant bank has committed fraud upon the accused, in connivance of the builder construction company, Kunal Structural Developers and Industries Pvt. Ltd. (henceforth, "the builder"). The accused does not deny availing the loan from the complainant bank but states that the same was advanced without verification of title of the flat sought to be bought by the accused, which was being developed by the builder under the head of "Nikhil Woodland Apartment". The accused also submits that a tripartite agreement, Ex. DW-1/4, was executed between the complainant bank, the builder and the accused wherein the complainant bank has failed to follow the RBI guidelines and has therefore connived with the builder. 17. The accused has further stated that the cheque in question was not issued to the complainant bank on 22.08.2016 but was taken as a security cheque from the accused at the time of availing of loan by the accused. He further states that there is no legal liability of the accused towards the complainant bank. The accused examined himself as DW-1 and relied upon the following documents: i. Copy of FIR against builder and complainant bank, Ex. DW-1/1 ii. Copy of Letter dt. 25.05.2017 issued by builder, Ex. DW-1/2 iii. Copy of Allotment letter of accused, Ex. DW-1/3 iv. Copy of Tripartite Agreement, Ex. DW-1/4 (colly.) v. Copy of Permission seeking mortgage, Ex. DW-1/5 vi. Copy of Allotment Letter of Ms. Barkha Agarwal, Ex.DW-1/6 vii. Copy of account statement of Accused from 01.08.2014 to 17.11.2014, Ex. DW-1/C1 viii. Copy of account statement of Accused from 27.11.2014 to 04.12.2014, Ex. DW-1/C2 CC No. 7842/2017 ICICI Bank vs Sachin Singh Thakur Page 8 of 29 18. It is made clear that the documents placed on record have not been objected to by Ld. Counsel for complainant and have, therefore, been taken on record and exhibited. However, exhibition of the documents are done only for the purpose of identification and does not suggest the admissibility of the same before this Court. Endorsement of an exhibit number on a document has no relation with its proof. It is the onus of the parties producing a document to prove each of these documents independently. Now, this Court shall proceed to examine the defences taken by the accused separately. DEFENCE TAKEN BY THE ACCUSED I. Defence of Authorized Representative of Complainant bank not being duly authorized to file the present complaint. i. The accused has stated before this Court that the Authorised Representative (AR) of the complainant bank, Mr. Lokesh Jaiman, had no authority to file the present complaint as his Power of Attorney had expired before the filing of the present case. Accused further clarifies that the document relied upon by the complainant bank to authorize its AR to file the present complaint on behalf of the complainant bank is the Power of Attorney, Ex. CW-1/A. Perusal of the same shows that point 9 of the said document reads as follows: "The aforementioned powers to do, execute and perform all and each of the acts, deeds, matters and things as stated above delegated to the Attorney for the initial period of TWO years or till the time Attorney remains in the service of the bank, whichever is earlier" ii. It is the argument of the accused that the Power of Attorney is dated CC No. 7842/2017 ICICI Bank vs Sachin Singh Thakur Page 9 of 29 23.09.2014, which accordingly, clearly expired on 22.09.2016, whereas, the present complaint was filed on 06.10.2016. This makes the present complaint unlawful as the AR had no authority to file the same on behalf of the complainant bank. iii. The legal position pertaining to this issue has been clearly laid out by Hon'ble Supreme Court in M.M.T.C. Ltd. v. Medchl Chemicals and Pharma (P) Ltd. , (2002) 1 SCC 234 saying that a complaint u/s138 NI Act filed by a person not duly authorized to do so, makes the complaint unlawful. It is stated as follows: "12. In the case of Associated Cement Co. Ltd. v. Keshvanand [(1998) 1 SCC 687 : 1998 SCC (Cri) 475] it has been held by this Court that the complainant has to be a corporeal person who is capable of making a physical appearance in the court. It has been held that if a complaint is made in the name of an incorporeal person (like a company or corporation) it is necessary that a natural person represents such juristic person in the court. It is held that the court looks upon the natural person to be the complainant for all practical purposes. It is held that when the complainant is a body corporate it is the de jure complainant, and it must necessarily associate a human being as de facto complainant to represent the former in court proceedings. It has further been held that no Magistrate shall insist that the particular person, whose statement was taken on oath at the first instance, alone can continue to represent the company till the end of the proceedings. It has been held that there may be occasions when different persons can represent the company. It has been held that it is open to the de jure complainant company to seek permission of the court for sending any other person to represent the company in the court. Thus, even presuming, that initially there was no authority, still the company can, at any stage, rectify that defect. At a subsequent stage the company can send a person who is competent to represent the company". CC No. 7842/2017 ICICI Bank vs Sachin Singh Thakur Page 10 of 29 iv. In another case titled Samrat Shipping Co. (P) Ltd. v. Dolly George , (2002) 9 SCC 455, Hon'ble Apex Court has held as follows: "3. Having heard both sides we find it difficult to support the orders challenged before us. A company can file a complaint only through human agency. The person who presented the complaint on behalf of the Company claimed that he is the authorised representative of the Company. Prima facie, the trial court should have accepted it at the time when a complaint was presented. If it is a matter of evidence when the accused disputed the authority of the said individual to present the complaint, opportunity should have been given to the complainant to prove the same, but that opportunity need be given only when the trial commences." v. Since a company or corporation can only appear through an authorized person in order to set the wheels of law in motion, it was the duty of the complainant bank to take due care and caution before filing of the present complaint. Therefore, applying the law to the present set of facts, it is clear that the complainant has chosen not to rectify their defect in the Power of Attorney till the very last stages of the case. This shows negligence and callousness on part of the complainant bank and the present complaint deserves to be dismissed on this ground alone. However, this Court shall proceed to examine the other defences taken by the accused on merits of this case. II. Defence of Security Cheque i. The accused has stated in his plea of defence, in his statement recorded u/s 313 CrPC and in his testimony that the complainant bank had taken 9 security cheques from the accused at the time of entering into the loan agreement, which has been illegally presented by them without taking prior consent from the accused and without giving due intimation to the accused. Therefore, it is the argument of the accused CC No. 7842/2017 ICICI Bank vs Sachin Singh Thakur Page 11 of 29 that since the cheque in question Ex. CW-1/B was not given towards a liability but as a security, the same has been misused by the complainant bank and that the present complaint deserves to be dismissed on this ground. Ld. Counsel for complainant has rebutted this point of the accused stating that the cheque in question is not a security cheque but a regular cheque issued by the accused towards part discharge of his liability to the bank. ii. The law on the defence of 'security cheque' is clear. In the case of Credential Leasing & Credits Ltd vs Shruti Investments & Anr. 2015 CriLJ 4273 Hon'ble Supreme Court has held as under: "30. Thus, I am of the considered view that there is no merit in the legal submission of the respondent accused that only on account of the fact that the cheque in question was issued as security in respect of a contingent liability, the complaint under Section 138 of the NI Act would not be maintainable. At the same time, I may add that it would need examination on a case to case basis as to whether, on the date of presentation of the dishonoured cheque the ascertained and crystallised debt or other liability did not exist. The onus to raise a probable defence would lie on the accused, as the law raises a presumption in favour of the holder of the cheque that the dishonoured cheque was issued in respect of a debt or other liability. As settled by the Supreme Court, the said onus obliges the accused to raise a defence - either by picking holes in the case of the complainant and/or by positively leading defence evidence which leads the Court to believe that there is a probable defence raised by the accused to the claim of the complainant with regard to the existence of the debt or other liability. The said onus does not cast as stringent an obligation on the accused, as it casts on the complainant, who has to prove beyond reasonable doubt the guilt of the accused." iii. In Suresh Chandra Goyal vs. Amit Singhal, Crl . Appeal Nos. 601/2015 decided on 14.05.2015, the Hon'ble Supreme Court had CC No. 7842/2017 ICICI Bank vs Sachin Singh Thakur Page 12 of 29 occasion to consider the defence of "security cheque". In this case the complainant invested monies, from time to time, in the business of the accused. The accused issued six security cheques of Rs. 50,000/-, which were to be returned upon payment of the corresponding installment. While three installments were admittedly received by the complainant, he claimed that the remaining three were not paid. The corresponding security cheques were banked; dishonoured upon presentation, and; after issuance of statutory notice, the complaint under Section 138 NI Act filed due to non-payment. The Hon'ble Court, inter alia, observed as follows: "28. There is no magic in the word "security cheque", such that, the moment the accused claims that the dishonoured cheque (in respect whereof a complaint under Section 138 of the Act is preferred) was given as a "security cheque", the Magistrate would acquit the accused. The expression "security cheque" is not a statutorily defined expression in the NI Act . The NI Act does not per se carve out an exception in respect of a 'security cheque' to say that a complaint in respect of such a cheque would not be maintainable. There can be mirade situations in which the cheque issued by the accused may be called as security cheque, or may have been issued by way of a security, i.e. to provide an assurance or comfort to the drawee, that in case of failure of the primary consideration on the due date, or on the happening (or not happening) of a contingency, the security may be enforced. While in some situations, the dishonor of such a cheque may attract the penal provisions contained in Section 138 of the Act, in others it may not." iv. It is clear that the accused cannot simply make a statement ipse dixit regarding the cheque in question being a security cheque and expect to have brought on record a probable defence in the matter. However, as it appears, during CE, the AR of the complainant bank has stated as CC No. 7842/2017 ICICI Bank vs Sachin Singh Thakur Page 13 of 29 follows: "Ques: Is it correct that the cheque in question bearing no. 000022 was given to the bank at the time of entering into the agreement? Ans: It is not in my knowledge. As per credit policy, one has to deposit four cheques at the time of disbursal of loan. One of the cheques is a cancelled cheque and the other three cheques are to be given as security cheques." v. This testimony of the AR shows that the AR is unaware of the particulars of the present case but does not negate the fact that security cheques are, in fact, taken by the bank in the event of housing loans, albeit at the stage of disbursal. This fact, although, does not prove that the cheque in question was a security cheque given by the accused but renders valuable information which cannot be discounted in favour of the accused. Therefore, the benefit of the doubt in this case must be accorded to the accused. vi. However, simply because the cheque was given as a security cheque does not automatically make the accused not liable for making the said payment to the complainant bank. This fact must be proved altogether independently by the accused in order to present a coherent and probable defence in his favour. Therefore, this defence of the accused is rejected. III. Defence of Inchoate Instrument i. The accused has raised this defence on the ground that the security cheques given by him were only signed by him but were undated and the amount in the cheque, either in figure or in numbers, was not CC No. 7842/2017 ICICI Bank vs Sachin Singh Thakur Page 14 of 29 filled by him at the time of handing over the cheques. Ld. Counsel for complainant has stated that the accused had properly filled the said cheque and handed it over to the complainant bank in discharge of his part liability towards the bank. This means that the accused has argued that an inchoate, or incomplete, instrument was handed over to the complainant bank which has been later filled up by the bank without the consent of the accused and therefore, the complaint based on such incomplete instrument is non-maintainable. ii. The law pertaining to inchoate instruments under NI Act is contained within s.20 , as follows: "20. Inchoate stamped instruments.--Where one person signs and delivers to another a paper stamped in accordance with the law relating to negotiable instruments then in force in 1[India], and either wholly blank or having written thereon an incomplete negotiable instrument, he thereby gives prima facie authority to the holder thereof to make or complete, as the case may be, upon it a negotiable instrument, for any amount specified therein and not exceeding the amount covered by the stamp. The person so signing shall be liable upon such instrument, in the capacity in which he signed the same, to any holder in due course for such amount; provided that no person other than a holder in due course shall recover from the person delivering the instrument anything in excess of the amount intended by him to be paid thereunder." iii. In the case of Ravi Chopra vs State 2008 SCCOnline Del 351, the Hon'ble Delhi HC has clearly explained the effect of non-filling of date and amount on the cheque where the signatures on the cheques have clearly been affirmed by the accused. "18. Section 20 NI Act talks of "inchoate stamped instruments" and states that if a person signs and delivers a CC No. 7842/2017 ICICI Bank vs Sachin Singh Thakur Page 15 of 29 paper stamped in accordance with the law and "either wholly blank or have written thereon an incomplete negotiable instrument" such person thereby gives prima facie authority to the holder thereof "to make or complete as the case may be upon it, a negotiable instrument for any amount specified therein and not exceeding the amount covered by the stamp." Section 49 permits the holder of a negotiable instrument endorsed in blank to fill up the said instrument "by writing upon the endorsement, a direction to pay any other person as endorsee and to complete the endorsement into a blank cheque, it makes it clear that by doing that the holder does not thereby incurred the responsibility of an endorser." Likewise Section 86 states that where the holder acquiesces in a qualified acceptance, or one limited to part of the sum mentioned in the bill, or which substitutes a different place or time for payment, or which, where the drawees are not partners, is not signed by all the drawees, all previous parties whose consent has not been obtained to such acceptance would stand discharged as against the holder and those claiming under him, unless on notice given by the holder they assent to such acceptance. Section 125 NI Act permits the holder of an uncrossed cheque to cross it and that would not render the cheque invalid for the purposes of presentation for payment. These provisions indicate that under the scheme of the NI Act an incomplete cheque which is subsequently filled up as to the name, date and amount is not rendered void only because it was so done after the cheque was signed and delivered to the holder in due course. 19. The above provisions have to be read together with Section 118 NI Act which sets out various presumptions as to negotiable instruments... 20. A collective reading of the above provisions shows that even under the scheme of the NI Act it is possible for the drawer of a cheque to give a blank cheque signed by him to the payee and consent either impliedly or expressly to the said cheque being filled up at a subsequent point in time and presented for payment by the drawee. There is no provision in the NI Act which either defines the difference in the handwriting or the ink pertaining to the material particulars filled up in comparison with the signature thereon CC No. 7842/2017 ICICI Bank vs Sachin Singh Thakur Page 16 of 29 as constituting a "material alteration" for the purposes of Section 87 NI Act. What however is essential is that the cheque must have been signed by the drawer. If the signature is altered or does not tally with the normal signature of the maker, that would be a material alteration. Therefore as long as the cheque has been signed by the drawer, the fact that the ink in which the name and figures are written or the date is filled up is different from the ink of the signature is not a material alteration for the purposes of Section 87 NI Act." iv. Therefore, in light of the facts of this case which are clearly covered by the above judgment, once the accused, i.e. the drawer of the cheque, has accepted his signatures on the cheque in question, s.20 of NI Act does not come to his rescue and the instrument shall not be deemed to be an inchoate or incomplete instrument in any sense. This defence of the accused in not tenable and hence, stands rejected. IV. Defence of non-receipt of Legal Demand Notice i. The next defence taken by the accused in his plea of defence as well as in his testimony is that he did not receive the legal demand notice, Ex. CW-1/D, allegedly sent by the complainant bank upon dishonour of the cheque in question. Ld. Counsel for complainant bank has objected to this defence of the accused on the ground that the legal demand notice u/s 138 NI Act was duly sent to the last known address of the accused through speed post as well as through a courier service and the receipt for the same along with tracking report has been duly annexed in the matter as Ex. CW-1/E and Ex. CW-1/F respectively. ii. The accused, in his cross-examination conducted on 29.01.2020, has admitted that his address, in 2016, was A-5/101, Block A, Pocket 5, CC No. 7842/2017 ICICI Bank vs Sachin Singh Thakur Page 17 of 29 Sector-17, Rohini, Delhi-85 and perusal of the legal demand notice, Ex. CW-1/D, shows that the notice has been sent on this address by the complainant bank. iii. In the case of N. Parameswaran Unni v. G. Kannan , (2017) 5 SCC 737 the Hon'ble SC has clarified its position regarding the service of legal demand notice in cases u/s 138 NI Act as follows:- "13. It is clear from Section 27 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 and Section 114 of the Evidence Act, 1872, that once notice is sent by registered post by correctly addressing to the drawer of the cheque, the service of notice is deemed to have been effected. Then requirements under proviso (b) of Section 138 stand complied, if notice is sent in the prescribed manner. However, the drawer is at liberty to rebut this presumption." iv. Therefore, once the complainant bank has sufficiently proved on record that the legal demand notice was sent to the correct address of the accused, the service of notice is deemed to have been effected. Furthermore, this point of law has also been clarified by Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of C.C. Alavi Haji vs Palapetty Muhammed , (2007) 14 SCC 750, wherein the Hon'ble Apex Court has held that no "service" is required for statutory compliance of ingredients of s.138 NI Act and compliance consists only of the notice being so sent to the accused persons. The part of the judgment relevant for this Court in deciding the present defence is as follows: "It is, thus, trite to say that where the payee dispatches the notice by registered post with correct address of the drawer of the cheque, the principle incorporated in Section 27 of the General Clauses Act would be attracted; the requirement of Clause (b) of proviso to Section 138 of the (NI) Act stands complied with and cause of action to file a complaint arises on the expiry CC No. 7842/2017 ICICI Bank vs Sachin Singh Thakur Page 18 of 29 of the period prescribed in Clause (c) of the said proviso for payment by the drawer of the cheque. Nevertheless, it would be without prejudice to the right of the drawer to show that he had no knowledge that the notice was brought to his address... The summons itself shall double as notice being sent to the accused and the accused persons can make the payment with respect to the impugned cheque amount as per the complaint under Section 138 NI Act within fifteen days from receipt of summons from this court and shall apprise the court of the payment so made, in lieu of which the complaint is liable to be rejected." v. In view of the above pronouncement of law, it is clear that even if the contention of the accused that legal notice was not delivered to the accused is accepted by this court, still the accused received the summons issued by this court and the accused did not make any payment towards the cheque in question to the complainant within 15 days of the receipt of the summons. This means that the ingredients of s. 138 NI Act were fulfilled and the complaint cannot be said to be non-maintainable. Therefore, in view of the above discussion, this defence of the accused does not hold any water. V. Defence of non-existence of legal liability towards complainant bank i. The next defence that has been taken on behalf of the accused is that the present complaint is not maintainable as the accused had no legal liability towards the complainant bank as no legally recoverable debt existed in favour of the accused, which would be meant to be discharged by the cheque in question, Ex. CW-1/B. CC No. 7842/2017 ICICI Bank vs Sachin Singh Thakur Page 19 of 29 ii. The facts of the present case, as alleged by the complainant, is that the accused owed the cheque amount i.e. Rs. 14,25,000/- to the complainant bank towards the liability incurred by the accused on availing finance facilities from the bank under Home Loan scheme vide. Home Loan Agreement no. LBDEL00002184163. It is observed, however, that the complainant has failed to place this loan agreement on record for the perusal of this Court. In the absence of the agreement or any other documentary evidence on record, the version of the complainant is left unproven. iii. The accused has stated the following circumstances as absolving him from the recoverable debt against the complainant bank: a) The complainant bank has violated RBI Guidelines in the sanction and disbursement of the loan to the builder. I. The accused has specified in his arguments that the complainant bank was hand-in-glove with the builder and that the bank took a route which enabled the builder to commit a giant fraud and that there are many other people, apart from the accused, who have been similarly cheated by the builder who was in connivance with the complainant bank. II. The accused refers to an RBI Master Circular-RBI/ 2014-15/ 6, DBOD. No. DIR. BC. 18/ 08. 12. 001 / 2014-15 stating that the LTV (Loan-to-Value) Ratio in respect of Housing loans should not exceed 80%, whereas, the complainant bank had sanctioned Rs. 42,75,000/- loan amount for a property of value Rs. 53,00,000 which is 80.6%, and therefore in CC No. 7842/2017 ICICI Bank vs Sachin Singh Thakur Page 20 of 29 contravention of the said circular. Ld. Counsel for complainant has not addressed this point in his arguments. III. The accused further brought the attention of this Court to the point that almost 99% of the sanctioned loan amount was immediately disbursed to the builder by the bank in a lump sum manner in contravention of the Tripartite Agreement, Ex. DW-1/4, which at point 4 clearly states that the bank shall disburse the loan to the builder in terms of a 'payment plan' agreed between the accused, builder and the complainant bank. No such payment plan has been annexed with the complaint by the complainant. IV. This fact creates a grim picture before this Court as the complainant bank has been unable to provide any clarification as to under what law a disbursement of 99% of sanctioned amount had been made to the builder. V. Furthermore, looking into the RBI guidelines that regulate the working of housing finance, in particular, RBI/2014-15/68 DBOD. No. DIR. BC. 18 / 08.12.001/2014-15 dated 01.07.2014 consolidating the instructions / guidelines issued to banks till June 30, 2014 relating to Housing Finance, has stated as follows: CC No. 7842/2017 ICICI Bank vs Sachin Singh Thakur Page 21 of 29 "3. INNOVATIVE HOUSING LOAN PRODUCTS - UPFRONT DISBURSAL OF HOUSING LOANS 13.1 It has been observed that some banks have introduced certain innovative Housing Loan Schemes in association with developers / builders, e.g. upfront disbursal of sanctioned individual housing loans to the builders without linking the disbursals to various stages of construction of housing project, interest / EMI on the housing loan availed of by the individual borrower being serviced by the builders during the construction period / specified period, etc. This might include signing of tripartite agreements between the bank, the builder and the buyer of the housing unit... 13.2 Such housing loan products are likely to expose the banks as well as their home loan borrowers to additional risks... 13.3 In view of the higher risks associated with such lump-sum disbursal of sanctioned housing loans and customer suitability issues, banks are advised that disbursal of housing loans sanctioned to individuals should be closely linked to the stages of construction of the housing project / houses and upfront disbursal should not be made in cases of incomplete / under-construction / green field housing projects. 13.4 It is emphasized that banks while introducing any kind of product should take into account the customer suitability and appropriateness issues and also ensure that the borrowers / customers are made fully aware of the risks and liabilities under such products." VI. It is clear that the complainant bank has not complied with the above circular and has acted in total disregard of the same. Ld. Counsel for complainant has not CC No. 7842/2017 ICICI Bank vs Sachin Singh Thakur Page 22 of 29 addressed this point to the satisfaction of this Court either in his written arguments or in his oral arguments. b) The Tripartite Agreement is null and void. Accused has stated that there is no liability on part of the accused to make payment to the complainant bank as the tripartite agreement which was signed amongst the accused, bank and builder is null and void in terms of Indian Contract Act, 1872 as the complainant has defrauded the accused. The onus to prove this defence lied solely upon the accused but he has not led any evidence nor produced any documents supporting this contention. Therefore, the accused has failed to prove this defence before this Court. c) The flat allotted by the builder to the accused was allotted to another person. The accused has stated that the flat in question i.e flat no.101, 3 BHK, (SBUA-1575 Sq. Ft.) was allotted to the accused vide allotment letter dt. 13.11.2014. A photocopy of this document, containing the signatures of the accused has been placed on record during Defence Evidence and it was not objected to by the Ld. Counsel for complainant. The same was taken on record as Ex. DW-1/3. The accused states that vide separate allotment letter dt. 22.08.2020 the same flat was allotted to another person, namely Mrs. Barkha Agarwal. This document was taken on record as Ex.DW-1/6. Ld. Counsel for complainant objects to this argument by the accused on the ground that no such information has been conveyed. However, the accused has failed to prove the said document as only a CC No. 7842/2017 ICICI Bank vs Sachin Singh Thakur Page 23 of 29 photocopy of the same has been placed on record and no witnesses have been called by the accused to prove the same. d) The complainant bank connived with the builder by not taking any conveyance deed or letter of possession from the builder. The accused has stated that the Tripartite Agreement signed between the parties to this case and the builder clearly specified in Para 2 of the same that the said loan shall be secured by a mortgage and that the said mortgage shall be created upon execution of Conveyance Deed, but the same was never executed. Ld. Counsel for complainant has stated that no such conveyance deed was required for the purpose of advancement of loan and that all the requisite documents were taken by the bank. This point raised by the accused does not count as a defence in terms of offence made out u/s 138 NI Act and therefore does not need to be discussed any further. e) The complainant bank has failed to explain how the liability in terms of the cheque amount has been fixed upon the accused. I. The accused has, throughout the trial, claimed that he does not have any liability towards the bank and that the money advanced under the housing loan should be recovered from the builder concerned. However, in arguendo, a pertinent defence raised by the accused is that even if the liability is fixed upon him by this Court, he did not have a liability amounting to Rs.14,25,000/- towards the bank on the date of issuance of cheque i.e. CC No. 7842/2017 ICICI Bank vs Sachin Singh Thakur Page 24 of 29 on 22.08.2016 and, therefore, the said amount cannot be claimed from him via this complaint. Ld. Counsel for complainant has argued that according to the repayment plan of the loan agreement, the accused had a liability up to the amount filled up in the cheque in question, towards the complainant bank. II. In reference to this, it becomes relevant to discuss the case Starkey Laboratories India Pvt. Ltd. Vs. Sanjay Gujral Crl . L.P. 492/2017 decided on 24.09.2019 which clearly states that when a liability of a particular amount cannot be established qua the accused, in terms of evidence placed on record, a cheque issued towards such liability cannot be recovered in a complaint u/s 138 NI Act. It has already been discussed above that the complainant has failed to place any such document on record which could help this Court to establish a liability upon the accused on the date of issuance of cheque i.e. on 22.08.2016. III. Furthermore, taking a look at the testimony of AR of the complainant, it becomes further clear that the complainant has been unable to establish the said liability onto the accused. The relevant para from the testimony of AR, in his cross-examination, is quoted below: "Que: Who filled the cheque in the amount of Rs. 14,25,000/- in August, 2016 when the pending EMI was Rs. 1,35,000/-? Ans: This is not in my knowledge. CC No. 7842/2017 ICICI Bank vs Sachin Singh Thakur Page 25 of 29 Que: How was the amount of Rs. 14,25,000/- in August, 2016 calculated when the pending EMI was 1,35,000/-? Ans: This is not in my knowledge." Looking at the evasive and ignorant responses given by the AR of the complainant bank, it seems plausible that the complainant bank had simply assigned the liability of Rs. 14,25,000/- upon the accused without bothering to calculate the same. This form of irresponsible behaviour cannot be expected out of a commercial bank. Applying the law to the facts and circumstances above, this defence taken by the accused is sustained. 19. Now, after discussing each and every defence taken by the accused in detail, we come back to the basics of offence u/s 138 NI Act. It is the most important ingredient of s.138 NI Act that there exist a "recoverable debt or liability" on part of the drawer of the cheque. It is true that once the signatures of the accused have been admitted, it gives rise to a presumption of existence of a legally recoverable debt or liability in favour of the complainant. However, this presumption is a presumption of law and not a presumption of fact. This presumption can be displaced by the accused by bringing a probable defence on record which would present such facts and circumstances before this Court that would render the version of the complainant implausible. 20. Referring back to the case of Credential Leasing & Credits Ltd vs Shruti Investments & Anr. 2015 CriLJ 4273, Hon'ble Supreme Court has upheld that the onus case upon the accused in cases u/s 138 NI Act is not as stringent as the one cast upon the complainant. Further, in the case of Kumar Exports v. Sharma Carpets (2009) 2 SCC 513, the Hon'ble Apex Court has held as under: CC No. 7842/2017 ICICI Bank vs Sachin Singh Thakur Page 26 of 29 "20. The accused in a trial under Section 138 of the Act has two options. He can either show that consideration and debt did not exist or that under the particular circumstances of the case the non-existence of consideration and debt is so probable that a prudent man ought to suppose that no consideration and debt existed. To rebut the statutory presumptions an accused is not expected to prove his defence beyond reasonable doubt as is expected of the complainant in a criminal trial. The accused may adduce direct evidence to prove that the note in question was not supported by consideration and that there was no debt or liability to be discharged by him. However, the court need not insist in every case that the accused should disprove the nonexistence of consideration and debt by leading direct evidence because the existence of negative evidence is neither possible nor contemplated. At the same time, it is clear that bare denial of the passing of the consideration and existence of debt, apparently would not serve the purpose of the accused. Something which is probable has to be brought on record for getting the burden of proof shifted to the complainant. To disprove the presumptions, the accused should bring on record such facts and circumstances, upon consideration of which, the court may either believe that the consideration and debt did not exist or their non-existence was so probable that a prudent man would under the circumstances of the case, act upon the plea that they did not exist. Apart from adducing direct evidence to prove that the note in question was not supported by consideration or that he had not incurred any debt or liability, the accused may also rely upon circumstantial evidence and if the circumstances so relied upon are compelling, the burden may likewise shift again on to the complainant. The accused may also rely upon presumptions of fact, for instance, those mentioned in Section 114 of the Evidence Act to rebut the presumptions arising under Sections 118 and 139 . 21. The accused has also an option to prove the non-existence of consideration and debt or liability either by letting in evidence or in some clear and exceptional cases, from the case set out by the complainant, that is, the averments in the complaint, the case set out in the statutory notice and evidence adduced by the complainant during the trial. Once such CC No. 7842/2017 ICICI Bank vs Sachin Singh Thakur Page 27 of 29 rebuttal evidence is adduced and accepted by the court, having regard to all the circumstances of the case and the preponderance of probabilities, the evidential burden shifts back to the complainant and, therefore, the presumptions under Sections 118 and 139 of the Act will not again come to the complainant's rescue." 21. Keeping in mind the above ruling, it is clear that the accused cannot be expected to bring on record negative evidence against all averments of the complainant and that the evidence placed on record by the accused need only fulfil the criteria of 'preponderance of probabilities' in order to displace the initial presumption that had accrued in favour of the complainant. 22. In view of this Court, the accused has succeeded in displacing the initial presumption u/s 139 NI Act. Now, the onus shifts back upon the complainant to prove the offence u/s 138 NI Act against the accused on the touchstone of 'beyond reasonable doubt', as in a regular criminal trial. The complainant has neither been able to prove the existence of liability in terms of the cheque in question against the accused nor the factum of any liability being affixed unto the accused. 23. In view of above findings this Court is of the considered view that in balance of probabilities, accused has rebutted the presumption u/s 139 of N.I Act and has proved that the cheque in question given to complainant was not towards the discharge of legally enforceable debt or liability. On the other side, complainant has failed to prove its case against accused beyond the shadow of reasonable doubt. 24. Accordingly, accused Sachin Singh Thakur stands acquitted of the offence u/s 138 NI Act . Bail bonds stands cancelled and surety, if any, stands discharged.
